clue.text: Baby group starts with some trigonometry

indicators.note: A word that starts with something has that piece at its front, so the maths abbreviation leads and the rest is written behind it.

parts.note: cos is the short form of cosine, one of the three standard trig functions
a set is a group of things, the mathematician's word for a collection

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a toddler class. Both halves of the wordplay are maths words, which is the only reason 'group' is sitting next to 'trigonometry' at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Baby -> COSSET: as a verb, to baby someone is to pamper and fuss over them, which is what cosset means.

clue.text: Sportsperson physically flexible and cold at the top

indicators.note: In a down entry the top is the first square, so the letter named beside these words opens the answer rather than closing it.

parts.note: C is the standard abbreviation for cold, the letter on a tap
limber describes a body that bends and stretches easily

explanation.walkthrough: The clue names the supple half first and only then says where the cold letter goes, which is a habit of down clues worth getting used to.
explanation.definitionFit: Sportsperson -> CLIMBER: definition by example, since climbing is one sport among many and anyone competing in it answers to the word.

clue.text: Scot mostly takes His Majesty for a fool

indicators.note: Most of a word is all of it bar the final letter, so the last character goes before anything else happens.
Someone who takes a visitor in keeps them indoors, so the letters named next are lodged within the word beside them.

parts.note: SCOT drops its last letter, and what remains opens up after its first two
HM is the formal abbreviation for His Majesty, as in HM Government

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing here is Scottish once the clue is parsed. The word itself is American slang out of Yiddish, which is why an insult this blunt can be clued so briskly.
explanation.definitionFit: a fool -> SCHMO: American slang, from Yiddish, for a dull and gullible nobody — the sort of person things get done to.

clue.text: Ground elder's back — what, more soil improver?

indicators.note: ground as the past participle of grind: crushed, so the letters are broken up and rearranged
the back of a word is its last letter, so elder gives up only its final one

parts.note: the word elder, with 's as the possessive

explanation.surface: A gardener grinds up ground elder, a stubborn weed, and wonders what else will enrich the soil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ground elder' reads as the weed, but 'Ground' is the anagram signal. R, the back of 'elder', joins WHAT and MORE to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Earthworms aerate and fertilise the ground by burrowing and casting, so gardeners prize them for enriching soil.

clue.text: Hit with tear gas from behind, quietly scarper

indicators.note: A thing seen from behind shows its back end first, so the word just built is written out in reverse.

parts.note: someone hit with tear gas has been MACED, and that word is turned round here
p is piano in music, the mark telling a player to be quiet

explanation.walkthrough: Mace is a brand of tear-gas spray that became a verb for using it, so five of the six letters arrive in one word before it is spun round.
explanation.definitionFit: scarper -> DECAMP: scarper is British slang for making off in a hurry, and to decamp is to leave camp, then to leave anywhere abruptly.

clue.text: Senior member aching after party

indicators.note: What comes after a thing is written behind it, so the longing follows the celebration rather than leading it.

parts.note: a do is a party or function in British usage
a yen is an aching longing for something

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are short words hiding in plain sight: the party is the British do rather than a political one, and 'aching' has to be read as a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Senior member -> DOYEN: the doyen of a group is its longest-serving and most respected figure, from the French for dean.

clue.text: One half of Macclesfield stupidly admit criminal activity

indicators.note: Half of a twelve-letter place name is six of its letters, and the six taken here are the opening ones.
Doing a thing stupidly makes a mess of the order it should be in, and letters handled that way come out shuffled.

parts.note: the word itself goes into the mix whole, all three letters
Macclesfield is a Cheshire town of twelve letters, and its first six join the fodder

explanation.walkthrough: Half of a word means half of its letters, and nothing in the surface says which half — the count is what settles it.
explanation.definitionFit: admit criminal activity -> COME CLEAN: to come clean is to confess wrongdoing, washing yourself of it by finally telling the truth.

clue.text: Jersey put in the post with sale item

parts.note: to mail something is to put it in the post
a lot is the numbered item an auctioneer puts up for sale

explanation.walkthrough: 'Jersey' pulls hard towards the Channel Island, and the sale and the post keep that shipping picture going. It is the garment.
explanation.definitionFit: Jersey -> MAILLOT: a maillot is a close-fitting knitted top or leotard, and in cycling it is the coloured jersey a leader wears.

clue.text: Carrie having squeezed out four, mechanism to limit that?

parts.note: a contraption is a mechanism or gadget, and it opens up after six letters

indicators.note: Press four letters out of a six-letter name and only the outer pair is left standing, ready to be pressed into something else.

parts.note: the four letters inside the name go, leaving her first and her last

explanation.walkthrough: The definition's own noun is doing double duty: 'mechanism' names what the answer is and also supplies the gadget word the leftover pair squeezes into.
explanation.definitionFit: mechanism to limit that -> CONTRACEPTION: the whole business of preventing conception, so 'that' is the childbearing the surface has just described.

clue.text: Clashing plate host eats on

parts.note: a dish is a plate, or the food served on one

indicators.note: What a host eats ends up inside the host, so the little word after this one is swallowed by the word before it.

parts.note: a host is a great multitude, the biblical sense that also means an army
the two letters go in whole, between the multitude's third and fourth

explanation.walkthrough: 'Host' is the multitude, not the man handing round the plates, and that single word is where the whole surface picture comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: Clashing -> DISHARMONY: colours or opinions that clash are ones which fail to harmonise, and disharmony is the noun for that lack of accord.

clue.text: Help island cutting bananas

indicators.note: A knife cutting into something ends up within it, so the letter named before this word sits inside the word after it.

parts.note: bananas is slang for crazy, and the three letters open up after two
I is the standard map abbreviation for island

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a shopping trip and none of it is about fruit or holidays. 'Help' is the noun for a servant, not the verb it looks like.
explanation.definitionFit: Help -> MAID: domestic help is the polite collective word for a servant, and a maid is one, so the definition is a plain synonym in that household sense.

clue.text: Three types of buffet show indecision

parts.note: to buffet is to strike, so a buffet is a blow — the sense with no food in it
the other two are the ways a spread is served, and the pair comes with its own linking word

explanation.walkthrough: Counting a punch among the buffets is the joke: one word carries a strike and a laid table at once, and supplies every part of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: show indecision -> BLOW HOT AND COLD: to blow hot and cold is to keep changing your mind, veering between enthusiasm and reluctance.

clue.text: Underground shelter arrived at with input from Republican

indicators.note: An input is something fed in, so the letter this introduces is planted inside the phrase already spelled out.

parts.note: to have got to a place is to have arrived at it; the word splits after its first letter
R is the letter American usage prints beside a Republican politician's name

explanation.walkthrough: The politics is a decoy — no party is involved past the single letter — and the shelter is as likely to be a garden folly as a real cave.
explanation.definitionFit: Underground shelter -> GROTTO: a grotto is a small cave, natural or built to look it, which is shelter in the plainest sense of a roof of rock.

clue.text: Naff stuff primarily in gallery? Not so

indicators.note: 'in' puts that letter inside the gallery's name

parts.note: the Tate is the London art gallery

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the first letter of stuff is used

parts.note: its first letter is S
less means not so much, to a smaller degree

explanation.surface: Someone sneers at the junk on show in a gallery, then reconsiders.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tate is the London art gallery; S, the first of 'stuff', goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Naff is British slang for cheap, unfashionable and lacking in style, which is what tasteless means.

clue.text: Not drinking after a dreadful experience with old liqueur

indicators.note: Whatever comes after a thing is written behind it, so the abstinence follows the bad time rather than opening the answer.

parts.note: the article is taken as the letter it is
a mare is British slang for a nightmare, a thoroughly bad time of it
TT is short for teetotal, said of someone who never touches alcohol
O is the standard abbreviation for old

explanation.walkthrough: Reading it as one sentence about a hangover is the trap. It is four separate pieces, and 'old' is here only to hand over its usual letter.
explanation.definitionFit: liqueur -> AMARETTO: definition by example, since amaretto is one particular sweet Italian almond liqueur among the many the word could name.

clue.text: Agree to gold even if more money

parts.note: AU is the chemical symbol for gold
even if means though, and tho' is its clipped poetic spelling
a rise is the British word for an increase in pay

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing in the clue admits that the middle piece is shortened; the letter count is what tells you. The surface pretends to be a haggle over wages.
explanation.definitionFit: Agree to -> AUTHORISE: to authorise something is to give it official consent, the formal end of agreeing to it rather than merely liking it.

clue.text: Prisoner's muddled memo that's clear for Spooner?

definitions.note: The definition is a description, not a synonym: a clause naming a thing that is clear and taken with a spoon, which is why it cannot be swapped in as a noun.

indicators.note: Something muddled has been stirred out of its proper arrangement, and letters treated that way come out in a new order.

parts.note: a con is a convict, and the possessive apostrophe-s hands over a letter too
the four letters of MEMO, stirred into a different order

explanation.walkthrough: The capital S promises the Reverend and his swapped syllables, and delivers none. Read him as a spooner, someone wielding a spoon, and the clear soup is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: that's clear for Spooner -> CONSOMME: consomme is clear soup, and a spooner is simply someone eating with a spoon rather than the syllable-swapping cleric.

clue.text: M25 maybe spoken about little

indicators.note: One thing set about another goes round it, so the longer word here closes over the shorter one.

parts.note: an oral exam is a spoken one, and the word opens after two letters
a bit of something is a little of it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Spoken' looks like a homophone marker and is not — it is just the adjective oral, opened up. The M25 is the motorway ringing London.
explanation.definitionFit: M25 maybe -> ORBITAL: an orbital is any road that encircles a city, so the motorway named is one instance, which 'maybe' flags.

clue.text: Hebrew bible Ruth can attempt in part, reading backwards

indicators.note: Only part of the words is wanted, and the part meant is a run of letters sitting untouched inside them.
Follow the row the other way, right to left, and the letters of that run spell something quite different.

parts.note: six consecutive letters, read the wrong way, spanning the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruth' is a book of the Hebrew bible, so it reads as more of the definition rather than as the letters doing the work.
explanation.definitionFit: Hebrew bible -> TANACH: the Tanach is the Jewish scriptures, its name an acronym of the three parts — Torah, Nevi'im and Ketuvim.

clue.text: Hide boat with start of cyclone forecast

indicators.note: The start of a word is the letter it opens with, so one character of the storm's name is all that is taken.

parts.note: cyclone hands over its opening letter and nothing more
an oracle is a source of prophecy, one who forecasts what is coming

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hide' looks like a verb telling you something is concealed, and nothing is: it is the animal skin the little Welsh river boat is covered with.
explanation.definitionFit: Hide boat -> CORACLE: a coracle is a one-person basketwork bowl waterproofed with skin, so the two words name its material and its kind.

clue.text: Jockey in bar over Ascot where there are track-side views

indicators.note: To jockey for position is to shove and jostle until things sit differently, which is what happens to these letters.

parts.note: fourteen letters of fodder, exactly the length the enumeration asks for

explanation.walkthrough: Ascot is a racecourse, so 'track-side' sounds like horses. The track is a railway one, and the answer is a carriage built for watching it go by.
explanation.definitionFit: where there are track-side views -> OBSERVATION CAR: a railway carriage glazed for sightseeing, so the views are of the line the train is running along.

clue.text: 12's fast, making the top five

indicators.note: making the top means becoming the first letter, so the five takes the place of the word's opening letter

parts.note: rapid means fast
V is five in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Something is fast enough to finish in the top five.
explanation.walkthrough: '12' sends you to 12-down, TASTELESS, as the definition; V replaces the R at the top of RAPID.
explanation.definitionFit: Vapid means flat and insipid, lacking any flavour or spirit, so it is a synonym of tasteless.

clue.text: Male cat has caught rat, perhaps

indicators.note: What the cat has caught is held in its jaws, so the animal's letters close around the other piece.

parts.note: the animal goes in whole and splits open after its first letter
he is the pronoun standing in for any male

explanation.walkthrough: The trap is reading 'Male cat' as one thing, a tom. Split the two words and the sentence still works: the male is what the cat has caught.
explanation.definitionFit: rat, perhaps -> CHEAT: a rat is one sort of double-crosser, and 'perhaps' flags it as an example rather than a straight synonym.

clue.text: Infection small yet spreading

indicators.note: Something spreading goes wherever it likes and keeps no shape, and letters loose in that way settle in any order.

parts.note: S is the clothing-label abbreviation for small
three more letters of fodder, taken exactly as they stand

explanation.walkthrough: Four letters and every word working: 'small' is the size on a label rather than an adjective describing how bad the infection is.
explanation.definitionFit: Infection -> STYE: a stye is the small infected swelling on an eyelid, caused by bacteria in a blocked follicle.

clue.text: God's will supporting study into sin

parts.note: to be pro something is to be in favour of it, supporting it

indicators.note: One thing driven into another finishes up inside it, so the room named before this word is buried within the failing named after.

parts.note: a vice is a sin or moral failing, and it splits after two letters
a den is the small room at home you shut yourself away to work in

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a sermon and is built from three flat synonyms. 'Study' is the room rather than the activity, which is the piece most solvers reach for last.
explanation.definitionFit: God's will -> PROVIDENCE: providence is the divine care that orders events, so what happens by providence happens as God intends it to.

clue.text: Exclusive clubs get rid of head of diversity

indicators.note: The head of a word is the letter at its front, so only the first character of the noun following is used.

parts.note: C is the card player's abbreviation for the suit of clubs
to lose something is to get rid of it
diversity supplies its opening letter only

explanation.walkthrough: 'Head of diversity' is a job title in the surface and a single letter in the wordplay, and the sentence about a members' club depends on you reading the first.
explanation.definitionFit: Exclusive -> CLOSED: a closed shop or a closed circle keeps outsiders out, which is what calling a club exclusive amounts to.

clue.text: Sinister type didn't eat filling in pies

parts.note: the food you did not eat is what you have gone and left

indicators.note: The filling is what sits in the middle, so the outer letters of the word after this one are the crust and stay behind.

parts.note: the two letters in the middle of the word, with the crust taken off

explanation.walkthrough: The surface promises a villain and there is none: sinister is Latin for left, a sense heraldry still uses, so the type meant is a political one.
explanation.definitionFit: Sinister type -> LEFTIE: sinister means on the left in heraldry and Latin, so someone of the political left answers to it.
